To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the colour-magnitude relations of elliptical galaxies are not consistent with a pure metallicity gradient; (ii) an age spread of about 1-2 Gyr is required to match the observed colour-magnitude relations; (iii) this age spread is consistent with the observed redshift evolution of colour-magnitude relations, and (iv) the age spread can be explained either by a range of star-formation efficiencies or by a range of infalling gas fractions.
(i) the age spread is a necessary ingredient of any model for the formation of elliptical galaxies, and (ii) a range of C-eff is a necessary ingredient for the formation of massive ellipticals.
the age-metallicity-degeneracy in early-type galaxy spectra can be broken by combining the constraints from the [Mg/ Fe] trend and the colour-magnitude relations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the formation of elliptical galaxies, which are believed to be the most common type of galaxy in the universe.
the chemical evolution of elliptical galaxies, and the relation between the star formation history and chemical composition.
the chemical evolution of early-type galaxies and how it can be used to constrain their formation and evolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the colour-magnitude sequence is a consequence of the combination of a range in ages and a range in [Mg/ Fe] (or equivalently, a range in C-eff and a range in tau(f)).
the colour-magnitude sequence is due to a combination of infall of gas and star formation efficiency, with a mass dependence of each.
the colour-magnitude and age-[Mg/Fe]-mass trends in elliptical galaxies are best explained by the combination of a range of star-formation efficiencies and a range of infalling gas fractions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have broken the age-metallicity-degeneracy in elliptical galaxies by combining the constraints imposed by their colour-magnitude relation and their [Mg/ Fe] trend.
the age-metallicity relationship of early-type galaxies is not degenerate with the star formation history.
the observed trend towards higher [Mg/ Fe] in more massive early-type galaxies is a consequence of the longer time-scales over which the star formation in these galaxies occurred.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the age-metallicity relation of ellipticals is not a simple sequence but a complex combination of the effects of infall, outflow and star formation history.
the age-metallicity relation in elliptical galaxies is not a simple metallicity sequence, and that a combination of age spread and metallicity spread is required.

the observed [Mg/ Fe]-mass relation in ellipticals is not compatible with a simple model in which star formation proceeds in a single burst, but requires a scenario in which star formation is spread over a long period, and in which the efficiency of star formation and the infall time-scale depend on the galaxy mass.
